lessons.title: Introduction to Java Collections and Generics
lessons.description: Understand the Java Collections Framework, interfaces, implementations and generics.
lessons.content:
The Java Collections Framework provides interfaces and classes for storing, accessing and manipulating groups of objects.

Important interfaces include Collection, List, Set, Queue and Deque. Map is also part of the framework, but it does not extend Collection.

List stores ordered elements and generally permits duplicates.
Set prevents duplicate elements according to its equality rules.
Queue supports processing elements, often in FIFO order.
Map associates unique keys with values.

Generics provide compile-time type checking. For example, List<String> restricts the elements that can be added to Strings.

Collection classes store object references, not primitive values directly. Autoboxing allows primitive values such as int to be stored using wrapper types such as Integer.

Choosing the correct collection depends on ordering, duplicate handling, lookup performance, insertion requirements and thread safety.

lessons.title: List, ArrayList and LinkedList
lessons.description: Learn ordered collections, indexing and common list operations.
lessons.content:
The List interface represents an ordered collection that generally allows duplicate elements.

ArrayList uses a resizable array internally. It provides efficient indexed access and is commonly the default choice for general-purpose lists.

LinkedList uses a doubly linked structure and implements List and Deque.

Common operations include add(), get(), set(), remove(), contains(), size() and clear().

ArrayList provides constant-time indexed access in typical implementations, while insertion or removal near the beginning may require shifting elements.

LinkedList can insert or remove efficiently at known node positions, but locating an element by index requires traversal.

For most ordinary application workloads, ArrayList is a good starting choice. Use LinkedList when its particular deque or linked-node characteristics are beneficial.

lessons.title: Set, HashSet and TreeSet
lessons.description: Understand unique-element collections and ordering behavior.
lessons.content:
A Set is a collection that does not permit duplicate elements according to its equality rules.

HashSet is backed by a hash-based structure. It does not guarantee iteration order.

LinkedHashSet maintains insertion order.

TreeSet maintains elements in sorted order using their natural ordering or a supplied Comparator.

HashSet typically provides efficient add(), remove() and contains() operations when hash distribution is suitable.

For custom objects stored in hash-based collections, equals() and hashCode() must be implemented consistently.

A TreeSet generally provides logarithmic-time operations, while a HashSet commonly provides expected constant-time basic operations.

Real-world applications include storing unique email addresses, tags, permissions and product categories.

lessons.title: Map, HashMap and TreeMap
lessons.description: Store and retrieve values using unique keys.
lessons.content:
A Map stores key-value associations. Each key is unique, but multiple keys may map to equal values.

HashMap provides hash-based key lookup and does not guarantee iteration order.

LinkedHashMap maintains a predictable iteration order, commonly insertion order.

TreeMap maintains keys in sorted order.

Common methods include put(), get(), getOrDefault(), containsKey(), remove(), keySet(), values() and entrySet().

HashMap permits one null key and multiple null values. TreeMap's null-key behavior depends on its ordering configuration and commonly rejects null keys under natural ordering.

HashMap is useful for frequency counting, caching, student records and lookup tables.

When custom objects serve as hash-based keys, their equals() and hashCode() implementations must be consistent.

lessons.title: Queue, Deque, Iterator and Collection Selection
lessons.description: Learn queue processing, safe iteration and practical collection choices.
lessons.content:
Queue represents a collection designed for holding elements before processing. Many queue implementations use FIFO ordering, but priority queues use priority-based ordering.

ArrayDeque implements Deque and supports efficient insertion and removal at both ends.

Common Queue operations include offer(), poll() and peek(). offer() adds an element, poll() retrieves and removes the head, and peek() retrieves the head without removing it.

An Iterator traverses a collection using hasNext() and next(). Its remove() method can remove the most recently returned element when supported.

Removing elements directly from many collections during iteration may cause ConcurrentModificationException. Use Iterator.remove() or suitable collection methods instead.

Choose ArrayList for general indexed sequences, HashSet for unique values, HashMap for key-based lookup and ArrayDeque for stack or queue behavior.

The standard ArrayList, HashSet and HashMap implementations are not inherently thread-safe. Concurrent access may require synchronization or concurrent collection implementations.

quizzes.question: Which Java collection interface permits ordered elements and generally allows duplicates?
quizzes.explanation: List maintains element order and generally permits duplicate values.

quizzes.question: Which implementation is commonly preferred for efficient indexed access?
quizzes.explanation: ArrayList uses a resizable array and provides efficient access by index.

quizzes.question: Which collection is designed to prevent duplicate elements?
quizzes.explanation: HashSet implements Set and stores unique elements according to equality rules.

quizzes.question: Which Java interface stores associations between unique keys and values?
quizzes.explanation: Map stores key-value associations and does not allow duplicate keys.

quizzes.question: Which HashMap method returns a fallback value when a key is absent?
quizzes.explanation: getOrDefault(key, defaultValue) returns the mapped value or the supplied default when no mapping exists.

quizzes.question: Which collection maintains elements in sorted order?
quizzes.explanation: TreeSet maintains its elements in sorted order using natural ordering or a Comparator.

quizzes.question: What does Queue.poll() do?
options: Returns and removes the head or returns null when empty
Returns the head without removing it
quizzes.explanation: poll() retrieves and removes the head, returning null when the queue is empty.

quizzes.question: Why are generics useful in Java collections?
options: They remove the need for objects
quizzes.explanation: Generics allow the compiler to detect many type errors before runtime.

quizzes.question: Which method is appropriate for removing the current element while traversing an ArrayList with an Iterator?
quizzes.explanation: Iterator.remove() supports removing the most recently returned element when the iterator implementation allows it.

quizzes.question: Which statement about HashMap is correct?
options: It allows duplicate keys as separate entries
It does not guarantee iteration order
quizzes.explanation: HashMap does not guarantee iteration order. TreeMap sorts keys, while LinkedHashMap maintains a predictable order.

exercises.title: Manage Student Names with ArrayList
exercises.description: Practice adding, updating, searching and removing list elements.
exercises.instructions: Create an ArrayList<String> containing five student names. Add another student, replace one existing name, remove one name and search for a given student using contains(). Display the final list and its size.

exercises.title: Remove Duplicate Email Addresses
exercises.description: Use a Set to store unique email addresses.
exercises.instructions: Create a List<String> containing at least eight email addresses with duplicates. Convert the list into a HashSet and display the unique addresses. Explain why HashSet does not guarantee iteration order.

exercises.title: Build a Word Frequency Counter
exercises.instructions: Read a sentence from the user. Convert it to lowercase, split it into words and count each word's frequency using HashMap<String, Integer>. Print every word with its count. Test the program with repeated words.

exercises.title: Create a Placement Task Queue
exercises.description: Implement FIFO task processing with ArrayDeque.
exercises.instructions: Create a Queue<String> using ArrayDeque. Add five placement preparation tasks using offer(). Display the next task with peek(), process tasks using poll(), and continue until the queue is empty.

exercises.title: Debug Concurrent Modification During Iteration
exercises.description: Fix unsafe removal from an ArrayList.
exercises.instructions: Consider: List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4)); for (Integer n : nums) { if (n % 2 == 0) nums.remove(n); }. Explain why this modification pattern is unsafe and may throw ConcurrentModificationException. Rewrite it using Iterator.remove() or removeIf().
